title: Make up a polymer stock without fish-eyes: one hand stirs with a rod while the other sprinkles the powder in
instruction: Make up the polymer stock: get all of the powder in the shaker dissolved into the water in the beaker, then put the rod and the shaker back.
context: Water and wastewater treatment plant operators (O*NET 51-8031.00) make up polymer stock for jar tests and feed systems, and food batchmakers (51-3092.00) disperse gums the same way. Dry polyacrylamide is made down by sprinkling it slowly into the vortex of stirred water, 0.5 g into 200 mL for a 0.25 % stock, to avoid fish-eyes (911Metallurgist, "Dry Polymers"). Gums and polymers start to hydrate almost as soon as they touch water (Ingredion, "How to disperse gums"), so powder that lands on still water, or faster than the swirl spreads it, gels on its outside within seconds into fish-eyes: lumps with a tough skin round a dry core that never dissolve (Ross, "Eliminate fish eyes in your mix"), which leave the stock weak and clog filters and feed pumps. So one hand keeps the rod moving the whole time the other sprinkles; one hand switching between the tools leaves the water still for seconds each time.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A clear 250 mL low-form glass beaker, 7 cm across (6.6 cm inside) and 9.5 cm tall, holding 200 mL of water (5.8 cm deep), stands with its axis at x 28, y 0 in a fixed black rubber collar round its foot. A glass stirring rod, 15 cm long and 8 mm across with a blue silicone grip sleeve 1.4 cm across and 4 cm long round its middle with a collar 2.2 cm across under it (30 g), stands upright in a fixed wooden rest at x 28, y 13: a block 4 x 4 x 3 cm with a 1.8 cm square hole 2.5 cm deep. A powder dredger (a shaker with a side handle) stands on the bench at x 31, y -11: a round white body 4 cm across and 9 cm tall, a red screw cap 4.2 cm across with seven 3.6 mm holes in its face (top 10.2 cm up), and a red round handle 2.2 cm across and 5 cm long sticking out of its side toward the robot's right at 5 cm up (40 g). It holds 0.5 g of dry polymer powder, enough for a 0.25 % stock. The beaker and the rest are fixed; the rod and the dredger are free. The water and the powder are drawn by the task's model: a pale disk for each floating patch of powder, a white ball for each fish-eye, and a thin stream while powder falls from the cap.
scoring: The powder model tracks grams in the dredger, floating, dispersed, lumped and spilled from the poses each step. Powder leaves the cap once it points past 95 degrees from straight up, faster the further it is turned (about 0.07 g/s at 105 degrees, 5 g/s cap straight down), and falls plumb; the rod's tip moving through the water keeps up a swirl that wets floating powder apart; powder floating 1 s on still water, or heaped faster than the swirl spreads it, gels into fish-eyes that never go away (fresh powder landing on a gelling patch joins it). Powder coming out of the cap for 3 steps in a row (0.15 s) while no hand grips the dredger's handle or no other hand grips the rod's sleeve (tool point within 1 cm, fingers stopped by it) scores 0 for good: a dredger parked tipped over the beaker would dose itself while one hand stirs. At the end (held 1 s), 1.0 when at least 95 % of the 0.5 g dose is on the water (the stock within 5 % of its strength), at most 3 % of the dose (0.015 g) has gelled into fish-eyes or still floats, at most 0.01 g fell beside the beaker (wet polyacrylamide on a bench is slick as ice), the dredger stands on the bench within 10 degrees of upright with its foot within 5 mm of the bench, the rod stands back in its rest (tip in the hole, below the rest's top), every tool point and pad tip is 1 cm clear of both tools, and both arms are back home and still (each tool point within 3 cm of where it started); 0.9 for the same with the arms not home; 0 otherwise. Powder sprinkled before the stirring starts, during a pause of over a second, by one hand switching between the dredger and the rod, or shaken in turned over, lumps and scores 0; so do powder left in the dredger, spilled powder, the rod left in the beaker and a tool still held. Possible scores: 0, 0.9, 1.0. In a real trial, weigh the dredger before and after, wipe the bench round the beaker onto tared weigh paper, pour the stock through a 1 mm sieve and weigh the drained lumps, and check on the video that the rod was moving whenever the dredger was tipped past level.
run_limit: 2,000 steps (100 seconds at 20 Hz; the demo takes 849)
reset_notes: Empty and rinse the beaker and refill it with 200 mL of water; refill the dredger with 0.5 g of dry polymer and stand it on its spot, handle toward the robot's right; rinse and dry the rod and stand it in its rest; wipe the bench.
fidelity: The powder and water are a scored model, not particles: grams move from the poses each step (flow from the cap by its tilt, landing plumb, a swirl driven by the rod tip's speed in the water, wetting one grain-layer at a time, gelling after 1 s). A real dredger needs a tap or shake to flow; here tilt alone sets the rate. Real trials can use xanthan gum, which forms visible fish-eyes the same way.
